title: The Scientific Study of Life
mcqIntro: 18 questions. Pick an answer to check it instantly — a wrong pick tells you exactly what to re-read.

mcq.stem: Which question could science, in principle, answer?

options.a: Does a high-protein diet increase muscle growth in adults?
options.b: Is it morally acceptable to eat animals?
options.c: Is Beethoven's music more beautiful than Mozart's?

mcq.stem: A student notices that her houseplant is wilting and proposes: "The plant is wilting because the soil has too little water." In the scientific method, this statement is:
Which statement is a *prediction* derived from the hypothesis "My phone won't charge because the cable is broken"?

options.a: If I use a different cable, then my phone will charge
options.c: My phone won't charge because the charging port is dirty
options.d: Phone cables often break at the connector

mcq.stem: A hypothesis states: "Something is wrong with the electrical outlet, which is why the toaster doesn't work." A coffeemaker plugged into the same outlet works normally. What should happen next?

options.a: The hypothesis is rejected, and a new hypothesis should be formed
options.b: The experiment failed and must be redesigned
options.c: The hypothesis is supported, so the toaster should be plugged in again
options.d: The result should be discarded because it contradicts the hypothesis

mcq.stem: In an experiment, testing more than one variable at a time is a problem because it creates:
In a drug trial, the control group receives a placebo instead of nothing at all. The main reason is to:

options.a: make sure the control group also benefits from the drug
options.b: increase the total sample size of the study
options.c: keep the belief of being treated equal in both groups
options.d: test two variables at the same time

mcq.stem: Researchers test a sleep supplement: Group 1 takes the supplement and is told to avoid caffeine; Group 2 takes nothing and drinks coffee as usual. Group 1 sleeps better. What is the main flaw?

options.a: The sample size is too large for the results to be interpreted reliably
options.b: The prediction was not an if/then statement
options.d: Caffeine intake is a confound — two variables differ between the groups

mcq.stem: In the echinacea cold study, all 437 volunteers were exposed to the same cold-causing virus at the same time. This design choice is an example of:

options.a: controlling a variable to prevent confounds
options.c: testing several variables at once rather than one

mcq.stem: In Andersson's widowbird experiment, some males had their tails cut and glued back at the original length. The purpose of this group was to:

options.a: increase the number of long-tailed males in the population
options.b: test whether females also prefer short tails as well as long ones
options.d: separate the effect of tail length from the effect of handling the birds

mcq.stem: "Evolution is just a theory, so it's basically a guess." The error in this statement is that:

options.a: evolution is actually a hypothesis, not a theory
options.b: evolution has never been tested experimentally
options.c: theories in science are proven facts that can never be revised, whereas evolution keeps changing
options.d: a scientific theory is a broad explanation supported by a large body of repeated evidence, not a guess

mcq.stem: A researcher catalogues the genes of deep-sea bacteria with no practical goal in mind. Years later, another team uses that catalogue to design a new antibiotic. The first project and the second are, respectively:
A supplement company claims its product "boosts the immune system", citing a "rigorous clinical study". A lawsuit later reveals no study was ever conducted. This case (Airborne) best illustrates:

options.b: a claim invented by people who want your money
options.c: an honest error corrected by peer review
options.d: the danger of small sample sizes

mcq.stem: Andrew Wakefield's retracted MMR-autism paper is especially instructive because:

options.a: his data were real but his sample was too small
options.b: he fabricated the data for financial gain, and the fear he created still lowers vaccination rates
options.c: later studies confirmed a weak but real link between vaccines and autism in some children
options.d: the paper was never actually published

mcq.stem: One small study finds that a food additive causes memory loss; dozens of larger, well-controlled studies find no effect. The most scientific response is to:

options.a: trust the small study because it came first
options.b: conclude the additive is dangerous, to be safe
options.c: go with the majority of studies, treating the small one as a likely outlier
options.d: average all the results together and conclude there is a moderate effect

mcq.stem: A crystal in a saturated solution grows larger and has a highly organised structure, yet it is not alive. Why not?

options.a: It is too small to be alive
options.b: Growth and organisation are not characteristics of life
options.c: A thing must show ALL the characteristics of life, and the crystal lacks most of them
options.d: It does not move on its own, and movement is the key characteristic of life

mcq.stem: Which statement about evolution as a characteristic of life is correct?

options.a: An individual organism evolves during its lifetime if the environment changes
options.b: Evolution is a change in the genetic make-up of a population over multiple generations
options.c: Evolution requires that every individual reproduces
options.d: Evolution happens only in bacteria, not in animals

mcq.stem: All the frogs in a pond, plus the fish, insects, plants and bacteria living there, together form a:
Which domain contains organisms whose cells have a nucleus?

short.prompt: A friend claims: "Science has proven that graffiti is wrong." Explain what kinds of questions science can and cannot answer, and rewrite your friend's topic as a question science *could* investigate.
Using the observation "my desk lamp won't turn on", write a hypothesis and one if/then prediction derived from it, then describe an experiment that would test the prediction. Label each part.
State and briefly explain the two principles that should guide the setup of any experiment.
Define *placebo* and explain, using the idea of confounds, why a control group in a drug trial receives a placebo rather than nothing.
In 2005 a small study suggested an epilepsy drug might cure AIDS; a much larger 2008 study found it did not work. Explain what this episode shows about repeatability and sample size in science.
Distinguish a hypothesis from a scientific theory in terms of scope and evidence, and explain why the phrase "just a theory" misrepresents how the word is used in science.
A worker honeybee never reproduces, yet it is unquestionably alive. Explain how this is consistent with reproduction being a characteristic of life.
Place these in order from smallest to largest and define the three largest: organ, cell, ecosystem, tissue, population, organism, community. Then state which level is the smallest unit of life.

extended.title: Designing a supplement trial
extended.intro: A company claims its new herbal tablet, VitaShield, prevents the common cold. You are asked to design a rigorous experiment to test the claim, with 400 volunteers available.

parts.prompt: Write a testable hypothesis and an if/then prediction for the trial.
Describe how you would divide the volunteers into groups, and what each group would receive. Name the experimental and control groups.
Identify at least three variables that must be controlled (kept the same across groups) and explain what would go wrong if they were not.
Explain why you would use randomisation, a placebo, and blinding, and what each one protects the experiment against.

extended.title: Evaluating a miracle product
extended.intro: An online advert says: "DetoxPure bracelets rebalance your body's energy field. A clinical study proves wearers get 70% fewer illnesses. Doctors don't want you to know!"

parts.prompt: Define pseudoscience and identify two features of this advert that suggest the claim is pseudoscientific.
List three specific questions you would ask about the cited "clinical study" before trusting it.
Using the Airborne or Wakefield case, explain why a financial motive should increase your scepticism, and what eventually exposed the fraud in the case you chose.
Explain the role sensationalism plays in spreading claims like this, and how the Wakefield case shows that a debunked claim can keep causing harm.

extended.title: Is it alive?
extended.intro: A space probe returns from Mars with three finds: (1) a self-repeating crystal lattice that grows in brine; (2) a microscopic capsule of protein and nucleic acid that multiplies only inside terrestrial cells; (3) a single-celled organism that consumes chemicals, keeps a constant internal pH, divides, and whose populations change genetically across generations.

parts.prompt: List the six characteristics of life and explain why scientists use a list of characteristics rather than a simple definition.
Evaluate the crystal (find 1) against the characteristics and give a verdict.
Evaluate the capsule (find 2) against the characteristics, state the verdict most biologists would give, and name the Earth entity it resembles.
Evaluate the single-celled organism (find 3), give a verdict, and state which domains of Earth life it would most resemble if its cells lack a nucleus.

extended.title: From guess to germ theory
extended.intro: In the 1840s, Ignaz Semmelweis observed that far more mothers died of fever in a clinic staffed by doctors who came straight from autopsies than in one staffed by midwives. He proposed that "cadaverous particles" carried on doctors' hands caused the fever, and ordered handwashing with a chlorinated solution. Deaths plummeted. Decades later, this idea matured into the germ theory of disease.

parts.prompt: Identify Semmelweis's observation, hypothesis, prediction and experiment, and state whether the hypothesis was supported.
At the time, was Semmelweis's idea a hypothesis or a theory? Explain what had to happen for germ theory to earn the status of *theory*.
Semmelweis's colleagues rejected his idea, partly because it implied doctors themselves were causing deaths. Which concept from this chapter does their reaction illustrate? Explain.
Was Semmelweis's work basic science, applied science, or both? Justify your answer using the definitions of each.
